extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners referencing MPEP §2106 guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting the §101 patent-eligibility analysis (products of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas) including the 'markedly different' inquiry for nature-based products and the Step 2B inventive-concept analysis under Alice/Mayo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select the closest naturally occurring counterpart
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing a claimed nature-based product to what occurs in nature, examiners should identify and compare the claimed product to the closest naturally occurring counterpart (not to other adjacent or broader natural material).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse the counterpart with other material that may occur naturally with, or adjacent to, the counterpart (e.g., compare an isolated gene to the natural gene, not the whole chromosome). If multiple natural counterparts exist, select the counterpart most closely related to the claimed product based on examiner expertise (e.g., when a cloned animal combines material from two breeds, choose the most closely related breed(s)). For combinations that do not have a natural counterpart mixture, compare to the individual nature-based components (e.g., each bacterial species in a claimed inoculant). See Myriad; Ambry Genetics; Roslin; Funk Bros.; MPEP §2106.04(c), subsection II.C. If a claim is rejected as ineligible, it is a “best practice” for the examiner to identify the selected counterpart in the Office action if the record is not already clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics compared must be possessed by the claimed product
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate characteristics for the markedly-different analysis must be characteristics that are actually possessed by the claimed product, because the claim defines what may be patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify characteristics from what is recited in the claim language and from the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the nature-based product. A characteristic may be explicitly recited (e.g., the prefix 'deoxy' in 'deoxyribose' signals removal of a hydroxyl) or may be apparent from the BRI (e.g., nucleotide sequence or encoded protein in a claim to 'isolated gene B'). Unclaimed characteristics cannot contribute to eligibility. See Roslin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider structure, function, and other properties as appropriate characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate characteristics can be expressed as the nature-based product’s structure, function, and/or other properties, and are evaluated on a case-by-case basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-limiting types of characteristics courts consider when determining whether there is a marked difference include: biological or pharmacological functions/activities; chemical and physical properties; phenotype (functional and structural characteristics); and structure and form (chemical, genetic, physical). Examples: protein-encoding information of a nucleic acid; complementary binding ability of nucleotide sequences; bacterial properties such as infection of certain plants; ability to degrade hydrocarbons; alkalinity of a compound; ductility/malleability of metals; shape, size, color, behavior of organisms; presence of plasmids; chemical being a nonsalt or crystalline; nucleotide sequence/genetic makeup. See Myriad; Ambry; Funk Bros.; Chakrabarty; Parke-Davis; Marden; Roslin; MPEP §2106.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics must be changes from nature caused by applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: To be 'markedly different,' a characteristic must be changed as compared to the natural counterpart and cannot be an inherent/innate characteristic of the counterpart or an incidental change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must have caused the claimed product to possess at least one characteristic that is different from that of the counterpart. If there is no change in any characteristic, the claimed product is a product of nature exception. If there is a change and the change was produced by applicant's efforts, then the change will generally be considered a markedly different characteristic such that the claimed product is not a product of nature exception. See Myriad; Roslin; Marden; Ambry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changed functional or structural characteristics can support eligibility (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional or structural changes relative to the natural counterpart can demonstrate marked difference and thus eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: In Chakrabarty the genetically modified bacterium had a changed functional characteristic (degrading multiple hydrocarbons vs one) and a changed structural characteristic (additional plasmids), and was eligible. In Myriad, a full-length cDNA containing only exons (structural change in nucleotide sequence) was distinct from the naturally occurring gene and was eligible. See Diamond v. Chakrabarty; Myriad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidental or innate characteristics are insufficient (examples of ineligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all changes suffice — incidental changes or characteristics innate to the natural counterpart do not establish marked difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: In Myriad, isolation that removed covalent bonds but left the gene otherwise identical to the natural gene was insufficient. In Ambry Genetics, single-stranded primers with the same nucleotide sequence and innate binding function were product of nature exceptions. Roslin clones were ineligible because they were genetic replicas and claimed phenotypic differences were unclaimed. In re Marden rejected a claim where ductility was an inherent property. The analysis focuses on what is claimed; unclaimed phenotypic differences cannot make the claimed subject matter markedly different. See Myriad; Ambry; Roslin; Marden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for an inventive concept (Step 2B) — must be 'significantly more' than the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: After finding a claim directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, natural phenomenon, law of nature), evaluate whether the claim elements add an 'inventive concept' — elements beyond the exception that make the claim as a whole amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventive concept cannot be furnished by the unpatentable exception itself. It is furnished by an element or combination of elements recited in the claim in addition to the judicial exception and sufficient to ensure the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception. Evaluate additional elements both individually and in combination; consider all claim elements because an inventive concept may arise from a non-conventional combination. See Alice; Mayo; RecogniCorp; Rapid Litigation; BASCOM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider additional elements both individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate claim elements both on their own and together to determine whether they amount to an inventive concept sufficient to transform a judicial exception into a patent-eligible claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consideration of elements in combination is important because an element that is not significantly more on its own may be significantly more when combined with others (e.g., Rapid Litigation Mgmt. v. CellzDirect; BASCOM). The claim must be considered as a whole consistent with Diamond v. Diehr. See Alice; Diamond v. Diehr; Rapid Litigation; BASCOM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate inventive-concept inquiry with novelty or obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The search for an inventive concept under §101 is distinct from novelty (§102) and obviousness (§103) inquiries; lack of novelty or obviousness is not dispositive of the §101 inventive-concept analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have rejected substituting §§102/103/112 inquiries for the §101 eligibility test. Novelty of an element is of no relevance to whether the claim falls within §101 categories; a new abstract idea is still an abstract idea. Patentability under §§102/103 is neither required for nor a guarantee of patent eligibility under §101. See Mayo; Intellectual Ventures v. Symantec; Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics; BASCOM discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations that courts have found to qualify as 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain types of claim limitations have been recognized by the courts as qualifying as 'significantly more' when recited with a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-exhaustive list (courts have found these to qualify): (i) improvements to the functioning of a computer (e.g., DDR Holdings); (ii) improvements to another technology or technical field (e.g., Diehr rubber-molding with thermocouple); (iii) applying the judicial exception with/by use of a particular machine arranged in a particular way (e.g., Fourdrinier machine example); (iv) effecting a transformation/reduction of an article to a different state or thing (Diehr); (v) adding a specific limitation other than well-understood, routine, conventional activity or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (e.g., non-conventional arrangement in BASCOM); (vi) other meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a technological environment (e.g., an immunization step integrating data-comparison into a specific immunizing process as in Classen). See MPEP §2106.05(a)-(e) and cited cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations that courts have found not to qualify as 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain additions or phrasing do not transform a claim directed to a judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-exhaustive list (courts have found these insufficient): (i) adding the words 'apply it' or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer (Alice); (ii) simply appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities specified at a high level of generality (Alice; BASCOM discussion); (iii) adding insignificant extra-solution activity such as mere data gathering in conjunction with an exception (CyberSource); (iv) generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use (Bilski; Parker v. Flook). See MPEP §2106.05(d),(f),(g),(h) and cited cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element is not enough
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical or tangible implementation of a judicial exception (e.g., reciting a computer) is not itself an inventive concept and does not guarantee eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fact that a computer is a tangible machine is beside the point; claiming a computer-configured implementation could allow drafting around §101 if mere physicality sufficed. Eligibility cannot depend on draftsman’s art. Courts emphasize that mere physicality/tangibility does not transform an otherwise ineligible claim into eligible subject matter. See Alice.
